A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRACE work. All 23 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic, CartPole, UAVDT vehicle-turning, and CMU gait experiments, plus calibration, robustness, and ablation results in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds sample-efficiency, scaling, domain-impurity, mechanism-count misspecification, simplex-ablation, and heuristic-comparison results.

M1.justification: Section 5 and Algorithm 1 retain the shared encoder, domain-specific experts, training objective, least-squares projection, simplex constraint, and temporal smoothing. Figure 2's corrections align its notation with the existing method. Continuous parameterization and learned gating are suggested extensions, not implemented replacements.

E1.justification: The four dataset families remain unchanged. Appendices E.7–E.8 extend synthetic coverage to contaminated training mechanisms and transitions involving mechanisms absent from training. The additional application domains in E.14 are proposals, not evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: Appendix E.12 and Table 18 add centroid tracking and optical flow as evaluated UAVDT comparators. The existing NCTRL, TDRL, LEAP, iVAE, and PCL comparisons remain; updated publication years do not introduce different baselines.

E3.justification: New experimental designs vary training data from 40,000 to 400 trajectories per domain, test 50 mechanisms at latent dimensions 8, 16, and 128, and introduce contamination and incorrect mechanism counts. Appendix E.9 adds a 500-trajectory constrained/unconstrained comparison and negative-weight reporting. Existing benchmark protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Sections 6.6–6.7 and Appendices E.7–E.11 substantially expand analysis of data scarcity, capacity, sparse perturbations, training-domain impurity, duplicate or missing mechanisms, and the simplex constraint. These test practical assumptions beyond v1's retained noise, smoothing, trajectory-complexity, and two-stage ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions use ± reporting and retain the same Kolmogorov–Smirnov testing protocol in Appendix E.3. v2 adds result rows using existing reporting practices, without introducing run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial results for the new analyses. Examples include correlation 0.936 ± 0.033 at 50% mechanism contamination and UAVDT heuristic scores of 0.911 and 0.902 versus TRACE's retained 0.960. Appendix D.3 corrects 0.92 to 0.96. Figure 5 also changes displayed prediction traces while retaining its summary metrics.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.1–4.3 and their Appendix A proofs remain unchanged. v2 qualifies the capacity bound as sufficient rather than necessary, adds active-submatrix reasoning in E.11, and states the mechanism-contamination collapse threshold in E.7. These are limited mathematical additions, not replacement identifiability proofs.

C1.justification: The central continuous-mixture formulation, two-stage method, and joint-identifiability contributions remain. The conclusion adds claims of graceful degradation under impure domains and mechanism-count misspecification, and broadens applicability to large mechanism dictionaries with sparse activity.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of duplicate-expert ambiguity, failure on unseen mechanisms, conditioning-based diagnostics, sample-efficiency behavior, and the accuracy–interpretability tradeoff of simplex constraints. Appendices E.6–E.14 substantially expand applicability and future-direction discussion; the original proxy limitations were already present in Appendix D.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link where v1 only promised release, although the release promise remains in Appendix D.5. New appendices document contamination construction, mechanism-count configurations, and evaluation sample counts. Existing architecture, hyperparameter, hardware, and training-time disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: Appendix E.14 substantially broadens positioning through new connections and citations to attention, manifold clustering, counterfactual identification, forecasting, medical applications, recommendation, and multimodal agents. E.13 adds the Dynamic Bayesian Network connection. Publication-metadata updates to existing references are separate editorial changes.

P1.justification: The established narrative and most existing prose remain. v2 locally edits the abstract and explanations, rewrites the concluding limitations, adds acknowledgments and cross-references, and extends the existing organization with new subsections rather than extensively restructuring it.

P2.justification: Figures 1–5 receive substantial visual revisions, including corrected architecture labels, new markers and legends, and clearer CartPole labels and heatmap values. v2 adds Tables 4–5 and 15–18; Table 17 redisplays Table 4 with sample counts. Existing figures and tables also move as the main text expands.

improvement.justification: The added tests directly examine previously untested practical assumptions about pure training domains, known mechanism counts, and abundant data, while heuristic comparisons better contextualize real-world performance. These improve the empirical support. However, the broader scaling claims in E.11 are not reconciled with Algorithm 1's retained full-rank inverse or supported by revised proofs, limiting the overall gain.
